founded.what: The year a wine merchant of Reims set up a business under his name, by the house's own account; it moved to Le Mesnil-sur-Oger between the two world wars.

place: Le Mesnil-sur-Oger, Côte des Blancs, Champagne

kind.means: A négociant manipulant, a house in the trade's own word: it buys grapes from growers of the Côte des Blancs and beyond and makes the wine itself, and the Union des Maisons de Champagne lists it among the houses.

story: Delamotte dates itself to 1760, when a wine merchant of Reims, whose name the house carries, set up a business there under his own name, at the corner of the rue Cérès and the rue des Marmousets, by the house's account. Around 1786, with his eldest son, he took the trading name Delamotte Père et Fils. The house dates its second birth at Le Mesnil-sur-Oger, in the Côte des Blancs, to 1927; the chronology of the Union des Maisons de Champagne dates to 22 May 1939 the purchase of the brand and a mansion of the eighteenth century in the village, by the woman who took over Laurent-Perrier that same day, and the wines have been made there since. Its neighbour in the village is Salon, the house of one wine. In 1988, by Delamotte's own account, the house joined the Laurent-Perrier group, which the Union's chronology dates to 1989, and Salon joined it the same year, so the two became sister houses. From then on, in the years Salon declares no vintage, its Le Mesnil fruit has gone into Delamotte. Chardonnay became the house's mark, its Blanc de Blancs the wine to know. Old vintages of it, the 1970, the 1985 and the 1999 among them, were later released as the Collection, held on their lees for decades and disgorged on demand.

style.line: Chardonnay first and the Côte des Blancs throughout: the house's Blanc de Blancs, from Grand Cru villages and made in stainless steel, is the wine it is known by, fresh and chalky.
style.grapes: Chardonnay from the Grand Cru villages of the Côte des Blancs, Le Mesnil-sur-Oger, Avize, Oger and Cramant, for the Blanc de Blancs, by the house.
style.reserve: Moderate, by the house's sheets: a fifth of reserve wine in a Blanc de Blancs based on the 2017 harvest, 15 per cent in one based on the 2019.
style.vessels: Stainless steel for the Blanc de Blancs, by the house.
style.lees: Four to five years for the non vintage Blanc de Blancs on the house's page, 48 months on a sheet; about 36 months for the Brut.
style.dosage: Low and moving by release: about 6 to 7 grams a litre for the non vintage Blanc de Blancs on the house's sheets and merchants' listings, 6.5 for the 2008 vintage.

nv.name: Blanc de Blancs
nv.note: Here the cuvée the class sheet names is itself the wine a guest knows: the non vintage Blanc de Blancs, Grand Cru Chardonnay of the Côte des Blancs.

cuvee.name: Blanc de Blancs

first.what: The first vintage or first release of the house's Blanc de Blancs was not found in the sources read.

cuvee.rhythm: Made as a non vintage wine and, in declared years, as a vintage: the house's pages show the 2008, 2012 and 2014 vintages, and late releases of the 1970, 1985 and 1999.
cuvee.blend: Chardonnay alone, as the name says: a Blanc de Blancs is a white wine made from white grapes.
cuvee.sites: Grand Cru villages of the Côte des Blancs: Le Mesnil-sur-Oger, Avize, Oger and Cramant for the non vintage; the 2014 vintage, by the house, adds Chouilly and Oiry.
cuvee.making: The wine is made in stainless steel, by the house. The non vintage then rests four to five years on its lees before disgorging, well past the fifteen months the appellation asks, and takes a low dosage, about 6 to 7 grams a litre by release. In years Salon declares no vintage, its Le Mesnil fruit goes into Delamotte, by the accounts of Vinous and Tatler.
cuvee.lees: Four to five years for the non vintage, by the house; about twenty years for the Collection 1999, disgorged on demand.
cuvee.young: Lemon zest and green apple over fresh bread and nougat, with a creamy mousse, a touch of vanilla and a chalky, mouth watering finish.
cuvee.aged: With age the vintage wine gains depth from its long rest, and the Collection shows how far it can go; no note of an old bottle was read, so none is given here.

forms.name: Blanc de Blancs Millésimé
forms.note: The vintage form, made only in declared years from the Grand Cru villages, the 2008, 2012 and 2014 among them; the house's English pages call it Vintage.

forms.name: Blanc de Blancs Collection
forms.note: Old vintages held far longer on their lees and disgorged late, on demand: the 1985, and the 1999 about twenty years after its harvest.

cuvee.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius, the Codex's range for sparkling wine; no need to decant; a tulip or a white wine glass.

table.house45: Delamotte is a Champagne house dated to 1760, when a wine merchant set up under his name in Reims. Between the two world wars it moved to Le Mesnil-sur-Oger, in the Côte des Blancs. Its neighbour there is Salon, and in 1988 the two became sister houses. In the years Salon makes no vintage, its grapes go into Delamotte. The house is known for Chardonnay, and its Blanc de Blancs, from Grand Cru villages, is the wine to know. It is a fresher, readier way into the same chalk and the same village as Salon.
table.house10: Delamotte is the Chardonnay house of Le Mesnil-sur-Oger, dated to 1760 and the sister house of Salon.
table.cuvee45: Delamotte Blanc de Blancs is Chardonnay alone, from Grand Cru villages of the Côte des Blancs such as Le Mesnil-sur-Oger, Avize and Oger. It is made in stainless steel and rests four to five years in the cellar before release. In years Salon declares no vintage, its Le Mesnil fruit joins this wine. Expect lemon zest, green apple and fresh bread, with a creamy mousse and a chalky finish. There is a vintage version too, made only in declared years. I serve it cool, at about nine degrees, in a tulip glass.
table.sale: If you are curious about Salon, Delamotte Blanc de Blancs comes from the same village and its sister house, in a fresher, readier style. May I bring a bottle for the table?
table.cuvee10: Delamotte Blanc de Blancs is Grand Cru Chardonnay of the Côte des Blancs, made by the sister house of Salon.
table.cuvee20: Delamotte Blanc de Blancs is Chardonnay alone from Grand Cru villages of the Côte des Blancs, aged four to five years before release. It comes from the sister house of Salon, which sends it its fruit in years Salon is not made.

guests.q: Is Delamotte the same as Salon?
guests.a: No. They are neighbours at Le Mesnil-sur-Oger and sister houses from 1988, but Salon makes one vintage wine from Le Mesnil alone, while Delamotte's Blanc de Blancs draws on several Grand Cru villages.

guests.q: What does Blanc de Blancs mean?
guests.a: White from whites: a Champagne made from white grapes alone, which here means Chardonnay. Delamotte's comes from Grand Cru villages of the Côte des Blancs.

guests.q: Does Delamotte make a prestige cuvée?
guests.a: Not under a prestige name. Its rarer wines are the vintage Blanc de Blancs and the Collection, old vintages held on their lees for many years and disgorged late.

traps: Salon and Delamotte share a village and an owner but are separate houses; in undeclared years Salon fruit can go to Delamotte.
The class sheet prints (Salon) Blanc de Blancs for Delamotte: Salon is the sister house with a record of its own, and Delamotte's cuvée is its Blanc de Blancs.
Delamotte has no cuvée with a prestige name: asked for its prestige wine, answer the Blanc de Blancs, never Le Mesnil, which is Salon's.
Delamotte dates itself to 1760 in Reims, not Le Mesnil-sur-Oger: it moved to Le Mesnil between the two world wars, in 1927 by the house and 1939 by the Union.

sheet.label: Delamotte Blanc de Blancs
sheet.note: The label prints Delamotte and Blanc de Blancs and never Salon. The sheet's bracket files Delamotte beside its sister house: Salon is a separate house, with a record of its own and one wine, Le Mesnil.

cards.front: Delamotte: what wine does the class sheet give it, and beside which sister house?
cards.back: Blanc de Blancs. The sheet prints (Salon) Blanc de Blancs, for Salon is its sister house at Le Mesnil-sur-Oger.

cards.front: A Blanc de Blancs from Salon's sister house at Le Mesnil-sur-Oger: which house makes it?
cards.back: Delamotte, founded at Reims in 1760, which moved to Le Mesnil-sur-Oger between the two world wars.

cards.front: In the years Salon declares no vintage, where does its Le Mesnil fruit go?
cards.back: Into Delamotte, its sister house and neighbour at Le Mesnil-sur-Oger.

questions.q: A guest wants a Blanc de Blancs from the sister house of Salon. Which house's bottle do you bring?
questions.exp: Delamotte is Salon's sister house and neighbour at Le Mesnil-sur-Oger. Laurent-Perrier is the group the two joined, Ruinart and Taittinger make Blanc de Blancs of their own, Dom Ruinart and Comtes de Champagne.

questions.q: By the house's own account, in which city was Delamotte founded in 1760?
questions.exp: A wine merchant set up the business in Reims in 1760. The house moved to Le Mesnil-sur-Oger only between the two world wars, which is why many guess the village.

questions.q: Which grape makes up Delamotte Blanc de Blancs?
questions.exp: A Blanc de Blancs is white wine from white grapes, and Delamotte's is Chardonnay alone from Grand Cru villages of the Côte des Blancs. Pinot Noir alone would make a Blanc de Noirs.

report: Delamotte is not in the library, so every fact rests on the house's own pages, the Union des Maisons de Champagne or two secondary sources.
kind.code: the letters NM were not read on a label; the Hachette guide lists Delamotte's wines as NM and a rating site gives the same, so the code rests on two secondary listings.
The founder, the founder's son and the woman who bought the brand in 1939 are described, not named: their dates were not found in two sources.

The founding place follows the house, Reims in 1760; the move to Le Mesnil-sur-Oger is 1927 by the house and 22 May 1939 by the Union, so the spoken lines and the cards say between the two world wars and the story gives both.

The group: the house says it was joined to Salon in 1988, the Union lists Laurent-Perrier's acquisition of Delamotte in 1989; the record gives both, and the Union's 1939 purchase shows the Laurent-Perrier family held it before.
Salon's fruit going to Delamotte in undeclared years, which the library states, is confirmed by Vinous and Tatler Asia.
style.malolactic is empty: only Tatler Asia says the non vintage goes through it, against Salon, and no house page read states it.

Left out: the Brut's blend (a single merchant's figures), the first vintage of the Blanc de Blancs (not found, so cuvee.first.year is empty) and a dosage for the 2014; the non vintage dosage is given as a range because releases read run from 6 to 8 grams a litre.

The aged glass gives no note, since none of an old bottle was read; the Collection 1999's disgorging is dated 2016 by one source and 2019 by another, so the record says about twenty years after its harvest.
The first trap is the library's Salon trap word for word, so the two records read alike.

changed: founded.what, story, house45, traps[3], cards[1].back and questions[1].exp: the move to Le Mesnil-sur-Oger was dated 1939 alone; the house's own story dates it to 1927 (Wikipedia and Corney and Barrow agree) and the Union to 22 May 1939, so the story gives both and the spoken lines, the card and the explanation say between the two world wars.

story: the buyer of 1939 is the woman who took over Laurent-Perrier the same day by the Union, not the family that ran Laurent-Perrier; and the joining of 1988 now says Delamotte joined the group and Salon joined it the same year.
house45: from 1988 the two have been sister houses, a present state, became in 1988 the two became sister houses.
style.dosage and cuvee.making: 7 grams a litre became about 6 to 7 by release; the releases read run from 6 to 8 grams a litre.
style.reserve: less than a tenth in one release was cut, not found; a fifth for the release on the 2017 harvest and 15 per cent for the one on the 2019 stand, by two listings of the house's figures.
open: NM was not read on a label; the Hachette guide and a rating site list it.
Stainless steel for the Blanc de Blancs rests on the author's reading of the house; no search of the refuter's stated the vessel.
